en: Having bowed my head to Lakṣmī, Kālaka, and Sarasvatī,
as well as to Gaṇeśa and Śambhu, I shall declare the Śāṅkara instruction;
the fourth section in the Taittirīyaka is to be known as the one named Agni.
The section beginning with "graha" and ending with "sajoṣāḥ" is prescribed as the first question;
the two initial questions of the Agnikāṇḍa,
together with the final anuvāka, are cited by those learned in the Veda as the [first] portion.

Beginning with *iṣe* and ending with *apām antam*, twenty-three questions joined together are declared; those from the final section beginning with *deva savitar* and ending with *upayāma* are designated as the *yājyā*s.
The section titled Vājapeya consists of six anuvākas; [the first] belongs to Vipracit, while [the others] should be known as Samid-diśām, Samiddho agneḥ, Manve, and Praṣṭhya.
Furthermore, there is a tetrad beginning with Jīmūta, and likewise two Gāyatrī verses.

Those who know the Veda understand that the three *anuvākas* which exist in the fifth *kāṇḍa*— excluding [the others]— are indeed the *praṣṭhya*, while the *mahāpraṣṭhya* consists of the beginning of the question (*praśna*) "āśmann" and so forth, comprising five *anuvākas*.
The seers who proclaim the Vedas call these the *vikarṣa* section;
the *vihavya* section, beginning with the *vāja*,
is prescribed for the three *anuvākas* by those who know the characteristics of the Veda.
The three questions beginning with the tenth are called *iṣṭi-yoni*;
since a single word is employed with reference to the act of grasping (*grahaṇa*),
it should not be taken elsewhere, as it occurs [only] among those who possess the matted locks (*jaṭā*).
In cases beginning with three syllables, when another [suffix] is joined,
Karṇa stated that there is never an elision; furthermore, even when another [suffix] is joined,
an upasarga ending in the vowel *a* sometimes undergoes the change to *āt*.
If the sounds beginning with *oṣṭha* (i.e., *o*, *au*) follow, the vowel *a* is elided;
the *ṛ*-vowel that follows [the elided *a*] remains as a nasalized *svarabhakti* together with the following *r*,
and because of this, the subsequent *r* is pronounced with a tone, provided it follows a long vowel.
The letter *repha* is Kareṇu, the letter *ha* is Ūrdhvā, and *la* is Karviṇī; thus is the Svarabhakti described.
Lohāritā is *śe*, Hariṇī is *ha*, and Hastinī is *ha*.
One should touch the *haṃsa* (the letter *ha*) above the *ṭa*-group (*ṭavarga*), and likewise touch the *va* in the middle of the mouth with the tip of the tongue;
this occurs where a *svarita* is seen following an *udātta* and preceding an *anudātta*.
It should be known as *pipīlikā* when there is similarity of vowel quality (*savarṇatva*);
it is called *dīrghā-pipīlikā-dīrghā* when there is similarity between the two vowels;
and when there is a single word (*padaikya*), it is said to be *pākavatī*, following the other [type] as well.

In a *dvandva* compound, the vowel *o* occurs for the two syllables *horā*; in the word *yāti*, there is *ūrdhva* (the substitution of *ū*); and in the phrase "suvas tv api yas tām avidvān," there is no insertion of the *anusvāra*.
Indeed, this collection beginning with the letter *a* should not be understood as applying to non-Vedic (*anārṣa*) texts.

In the case of the two words *vyāna* and *udāna*, which end in a vowel and a consonant respectively, [the rule] beginning with "nityād" applies before the *yam*. After a root preceded by *i* or *u*, the suffix *etira* is applied. Wherever homogeneous vowels (*savarṇa*) are seen, as well as the *visarga*, [these rules apply].

It should be understood as *pipīlikā*; other than that, it is called "long" (*dīrgha*). Since the long vowel and the *guṇa* arise from a letter whether it is combined (*pṛkta*) or uncombined (*apṛkta*), both are substitutes for *ūbhau*; therefore, this applies even from the *saṃhitā*.

For it is the established conclusion that when the syllable *anu* is joined with the syllable *ukāra* and the letter *va* undergoes modification (*vaikṛta*) in the *jaṭā* formation, there is no elision of the vowel *a*;
indeed, this is seen at the beginning of the *jaṭā* according to the sequence of the *kāṇḍas*, as follows:
The operations of elision (*alopa*) and substitution (*upala*) apply at the beginning of a word-group of three or more syllables, as does the subsequent operation.
When a mantra that was previously stated is uttered again,
those respective operations must be performed exactly as before by those most learned in the Vedas.

This [treatise] effects the apprehension of the nature of *ṣatva* and *ṇatva* as taught in the grammatical instruction; it performs this function everywhere, and not otherwise. Thus, in examples such as *brāhmaṇāya* and *itopeta*, the phonetic combination (*akṣara-saṃhitā*) [is established].

Even there, because of the priority of the preceding [element], the *aikāra* (the single vowel *ai*) would not be possible here; however, just as in the case of *punaskṛdhi*, it is accepted by force when there is a reversal,
because of the priority of *punaḥ*, which serves as the cause for the application of *kṛdhi*.
In the *Aṅgulīsvaranirdeśa*, one should not indicate a defective limb as a limb;
rather, one should place the *svarita* arising from the *anunāsika* (nasal) upon another part of the limb.
When the *svara* arises, the *anusvāra* should be of the measure of half an *aṇu*.
There is a pause between those two [svaritas] that are specifically long; there is no *pracaya* after an acute (*udātta*) nor before it;
and after a *pracaya*, there is a grave (*nihata*) followed by a *pracaya*.
One should know that where a visarga preceded by a long vowel is seen at the end of a long [syllable], it is called "middle" (madhyama), and indeed a single mātrā is employed;
this is also known as the "vaiśeṣika" [pause] when occurring between two long vowels.
In the long yuga, the middle [measure] is seen as that of an ant; however, when there is equality in the following of the calves,
the primary [measure] is the middle-sized atom, which is the time of the pause.

One should indicate the *anudātta* (unaccented) vowels with the tips of the little finger, the ring finger, the middle finger, and the index finger, while the *udātta* (high-pitched) vowels are indicated by the tip of the thumb. It is traditionally taught that the *svarita* (circumflex) accent occurs when the [thumb] is bent down toward the base of the little finger and the other fingers.

The *pracaya* accent occurs in the middle; among the [five] positions beginning with the forefinger, the acute (*udātta*) is known to be in the heart, the grave (*anudātta*) at the head, and the circumflex (*svarita*) at the root of the ear. The *pracaya* is traditionally held to extend through all [the remaining positions].

A doubling of letters never occurs after the letter *ra* or the letter *ha*, nor after the second letter of a consonant class (*varga*), nor under any circumstances after the fourth letter of a class. Furthermore, when *naṅ* (nasals) occur at the end of a word, a doubling does not take place even when followed by *ya*, *va*, *ha*, or *eṣ*.
The two [nasals] do not undergo doubling when followed by *naṅ* or *vyadṛ*, except when followed by *repha*; likewise, a *repha* following a long vowel, a *repha* situated after a short vowel,
a *repha* following a high-pitched (*udātta*) vowel with an *ṛ*-sound, a circumflex (*svarita*) vowel, or a protracted (*pracaya*) high-pitched vowel [do not double].

There is no *pracaya* (prolongation) at the beginning of a word; therefore, when a vowel follows within a single word, the acute (*udātta*) accent is also not to be recognized in the act of placing the hand [on the syllables]. At the time of reciting the *pada-pāṭha*, when a word-final *m* stands before a labial consonant (*pavarga*), [the following rules apply].
Furthermore, the seers who proclaim the Vedas say that there is a renewed effort (*prayatna*);
thus it is well known in the sequence of the *jaṭā*, and even in the words of the seers,
when there is a conjunction with the labial class (*pavarga*), a separate effort is not required for *oṃ*.

From the letter *ma*, the mind does not proceed upward through the enclosure above the labial class (*pavarga*); it strikes the fire of the body, which impels the vital air (*māruta*). Moving within the chest, that vital air produces the deep, resonant tone (*mandra*).
At the beginning of a *praśna*, an *anuvāka*, or the like, the syllable "hariḥ" should be uttered with the *visarga*;
at the beginning of the *praṇava*, it should be joined with euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*); and at the conclusion, it should be *svarita*.
In the middle of the injunction (*vidhi*), it should be nasalized; thus, no contradiction is recorded in the tradition.
Therefore, it is indeed the *dharma* of the castes that performs their duties. That which is the object of the senses is called "syllable" (*aṇu*) by the wise;
its measure is traditionally held to be four such syllables.
A *raṅgapluta* consists of four *mātrās*, a *śuddhapluta* consists of three *mātrās*,
a long vowel (*dīrgha*) pronounced with high pitch (*ucca*) consists of two *mātrās*, and a short vowel (*hrasva*) consists of one *mātrā*.
This applies if there occurs a conjunction (*saṃyoga*) of consonants (*sparśa*) with one another.
If there were no initial *śruti* for those two, nor the finality of the consonant,
and if the former were infinite and the latter were at the end,
that which stands between them would be called the nasal place (*nāsikā-sthāna*).
Through association with the five *haś* sounds, there is nasality (*nāsikyātva*) and thoracic quality (*aurasyatva*);

through association with the semivowels (*antasthā*), there is thoracic quality; but for the [sound] *ka* alone, when followed by a sibilant (*ūṣman*) and situated at the beginning or middle of a word, there is guttural quality (*kāṇṭhyatva*).
A wise person should first establish the secondness of the first;
even in the case of *dhūṅkṣṇā daṅkṣṇavaḥ*, the anusvāra occurs according to its distinct property (*vidharma*).
Thus ends the Śambhuśikṣā.
